# ANDREAE’S / MENIPPUS

<note>original: "Andreæ / Menippus". Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654) was a prominent German theologian and social critic. The title "Menippus" refers to a style of "Menippean satire," named after the Greek philosopher Menippus of Gadara. This genre typically uses a mixture of prose and verse to mock intellectual pretension and social folly.</note>

<meta>The handwritten title on the spine is reconstructed from fragments as: [JOHAN]NES [VALEN]TINI [ANDRE]AE [MENIP]PUS.</meta>

# THE ANTIPODES.
<note>original: "Antipodes" — Historically, this referred to people living on the opposite side of the earth, often used here metaphorically to address those with a different perspective or perhaps a "topsy-turvy" world.</note>
### Greetings, good, simple, and wise men.

I send to you, my excellent friends, an image of our hemisphere, drawn not with the brush of **Apelles** <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, known for his incredible realism.</note> but with a chance piece of charcoal. There is no hope of profit from you, except for the desire to compare these things with your own affairs. Come then, if there is anything among you equally or less absurd, share it, since we have all obtained the same most rugged globe. There is no refined style here except for <term>parrhesia</term> <note>original: "parrhiſia" — A Greek term meaning "boldness" or "freedom of speech," specifically the obligation to speak the truth for the common good even at personal risk.</note>, and no authors cited other than eyes, ears, and touch. My modesty has held back any professional praiser; the Sun is my witness, whom I have prayed to be my messenger to you. Live well and have pity. Written in the North, at an elevation of 50 degrees from the pole. <note>This likely places the author in Northern Europe, perhaps Germany or England.</note>

->Farewell.<-
->*Menippus.*<-
<note>Menippus was a 3rd-century BCE Greek satirist known for mocking the foibles of philosophers and elites; his name here is a pseudonym suggesting the work is a "Menippean Satire."</note>

Although in every age the pursuit of truth has been as great as the hatred of it—and while that pursuit has never been suppressed even among the most savage of men, that hatred in the brightest [light]... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

# PREFACE

*...[maintained] in a light never interrupted; however, there has rarely been an equal regard for both among men, and the freedom of speech <note>original: "libertas linguae"</note> has remained harmless only among a very few judges of human affairs and of time. For since the actions of the worldly stage <note>original: "mundanae scenae"; a reference to the 'Theatrum Mundi' or the world as a theater where humans are merely actors</note> are repeatedly plunged—as if by a natural motion—from light into darkness, and from reason into the conflicts of opinions, it has never been safe to speak out against the rushing decline of men, let alone to wish to resist such a leaning mass. Therefore, however many have undertaken the defense of truth—perhaps invited by the good fortune of the times or the leniency of princes—they have scarcely freed her enough, or for long, from the tyranny of opinions. Instead, having displayed their effort in a praiseworthy cause, as soon as they noticed the business was as dangerous as it was laborious, they were satisfied merely to have expressed their thoughts without being punished. This is why those most ingenious labors of the Philosophers were in vain—labors in which they wished for the heavens, lands, seas, and man himself to be recalled to and examined by the standard <term>amussim: a carpenter’s rule or level, used here metaphorically to mean a strict standard of measurement</term> of truth and goodness. Great volumes were completed for this purpose, yet the dizziness of the human brain, the slipperiness of changeable time, and the instability of this machine of ours <note>original: "machinae hujus nostrae"; likely referring to the human body or the physical world system</note> always prevailed, until our Christ, the truth and goodness itself and the salvation of the world,*

<summary>This page describes the historical difficulty of speaking truth in a world governed by shifting opinions and political danger, noting that even the greatest philosophers failed to establish a permanent standard of truth until the coming of Christ.</summary>
<keywords>freedom of speech, tyranny of opinion, worldly stage, philosophers, standard of truth, human fragility, Christ</keywords>

-># TO THE READER<-

...walking about, and crying out nothing to the World <note>original: "Mundum"; here referring to the secular or material realm</note>, has clearly shown us that there is no reason why we should hope for anything further from it, or expend our labors unless in vain. It is, of course, a kingdom of darkness and of whirlwinds, where whatever you might attempt, "Ethiopians never turn white" <note>A common Latin proverb, "Aethiopem lavare" (to wash an Ethiopian), meaning to labor in vain or to attempt to change an unchangeable nature</note>, and the blind cannot be delighted by light. Yet, the world must be rebuked so that when He comes to decree the final sentence upon every individual at the Last Judgment <note>original: "supremo Judicio"</note>, the conscience may be tormented by the memory of the truth it once heard. 

From that time on, every virtuous person, struggling against the hatred of Satan, has gone forth to provide for his own through the confession of truth. For this one name—ever mocked and frequently accused—he has irrigated the fields of the Church <note>original: "Ecclesiae"</note> with faithful blood. This continued until we, having sunk down to the dregs <note>original: "feces"</note> of the earthly world, have been left with such a great amount of conflict from both sides that we labor most desperately under the sheer multitude of arguments and the difficulty of choosing between them.

Consequently, many people, frightened away from any more serious struggle, easily turn to complaints; and as if treated most unfairly, they impatiently and riotously pour out whatever first "comes into their mouths" <note>original: "in buccam venit"; a Latin idiom meaning to speak impulsively or without reflection</note>. They feel sufficiently relieved if someone at least hears their lamentations without taking offense, even if that person provides no actual support or help. For since, under the brightest [light] of the Gospel light <note>original: "Evangelicae lucis"</note> and of the excel-

-># PREFACE<-

...[treated most unfairly despite] the restoration of the most excellent things, for which the Blessed Luther <note>original: "B. Lutherus"; refers to Martin Luther, the central figure of the Protestant Reformation, whom the author styles as a "Hero"</note>, the invincible hero of our century, fought so hard alongside so many other illustrious champions <note>original: "athletis"; used here in the classical sense of "contestants" or "fighters" for a cause</note>. Instead, we are being thrust down by great tyranny and foul deception into mere blemishes, paganisms, fantasies, dross, and ghosts. We are not permitted to defend the honors of Christianity, of learning, or of humanity, except by merely boasting of the name; rather, we are perpetually exposed to the mockery and whim of those who control the stage of this **Worldly Drama** <note>original: "Mundanae fabulae"; a common Renaissance metaphor for life and politics as a theatrical performance</note>. 

Let no one wonder, then, that among so many prisons and chains, our sobs and murmurs are sometimes heard; and since all hope of improvement or liberation is gone, these words escape us as a consolation and a means to distract us from our weariness. Our present work is something of this kind: it complains in various ways about many things afflicting our affairs, whether sacred or secular. Yet, it is by no means directed against our Religion—which has been cleansed by divine gift and stands invincible through the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, delivered to Emperor Charles V in 1530</note> and its harmonious explanation—nor against the most honorable laws by which the most praised virtues are governed, nor against the decent orders of human life, the distinctions of which form the basis of Christian society, nor against the most elegant arts, through whose service the human mind [is refined]...

<summary>The author laments the current state of the world as a "theatrical drama" of tyranny and deception, despite the theological restorations of Martin Luther. He clarifies that his writings are a form of consolation for the weary, not an attack on the established Lutheran faith or the social order.</summary>

<keywords>Martin Luther, Augsburg Confession, Reformation, Worldly Drama, Christian society, religious struggle, consolation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader." The previous page's catchword "expli-" is completed here as "explicat" (explains). -># TO THE READER<-

...explains the injustice. For no matter how beneficial these things are for the human race, human tyranny and cunning have not spared them. Instead, by entangling itself in them, this tyranny has abused them to work against human nobility and peace. Thus, it was easy to point out specific details in each instance so that the unfairness of the situation or the obviousness of the trickery might be revealed even to simple folk. Just as a blemish is easily noticed on a beautiful face, so this work shows the true clarity and purity of our Christianity <note>original: "Christianismus"; here referring to the core essence of the Christian faith</note>, while simultaneously exposing every indignity and fraud, setting them before human society to be scrutinized.

The purpose of this is by no means to make those who deserve so ill grow mild or feel shame, nor to lessen the public's opinion of them. Nonetheless, it is satisfying for us to demonstrate that they can never hide themselves or shroud themselves in darkness so completely that some part of their foulness is not exposed to us. Indeed, the acknowledged truth is the only chain that can drag them, even against their will, out of their hiding places. For just as a suffered injury calls the rest of mankind out from their secret places, so does this unvarnished truth <note>original: "agrestis veritas"; literally "wild" or "rustic" truth, implying truth that is raw and unrefined by courtly or academic deception</note> provoke these men. They are forced either to fight against it or—the thing they dread most—to go hungry. Therefore, while such men speak of and threaten us with evils, we [uphold] the Church of God and the Christian...

<meta>This page concludes the preface "To the Reader." It continues the final sentence from the previous page, where the author began an appeal to various authorities to justify his work and the criticisms contained within it.</meta>

-># PREFACE TO THE READER<-

...implore the **Christian commonwealth** <note>original: "Christianam rempublicam"; a common term for the unified body of Christian nations and people</note>, as well as human scholarship and all reason alike: since we seek nothing at all except the harmony of life and doctrine, the combined observation of the present and the past, and a truer interpretation of nature. Furthermore, we rebuke no one, except those who are openly hostile toward our labors, our expenses, and our patience. Let them allow us, in this *noisy and scribbling age* <note>original: "strepero & scripturiente seculo"; the author is commenting on the explosion of printed pamphlets and loud public debates in the 17th century</note>, to have indulged somewhat in complaints. 

For if hirelings accuse us entirely of heresy, and if they charge us as traitors to the fatherland with <term>high treason</term> <note>original: "perduellionis"; a specific legal term for crimes against the state or its ruler</note>, and if those most ignorant of languages and arts charge us with barbarism—let us bear it with the good God, and let us set this one saying against them: *“If the world had not declared them heretics, Christ would have no martyrs.”*

But you, **honest Reader**, who walk freely like a wise traveler in the marketplace of my *World* <note>original: "Orbis mei foro"; likely referring to the book itself as an encyclopedia or map of knowledge</note>, when you have examined those men and heard our side, and have carefully weighed the whole matter in your mind: if we seem too impatient, rebuke us freely; but if we persuade you that we have accused justly, have pity on us. Finally, mindful of yourself and of the good people who labor, go forth to the task enjoined by God. 

**Farewell.**

# 1. ENCYCLOPEDIA. <note>From the Greek "enkyklios paideia," meaning a "circle of education" or a well-rounded curriculum of all arts and sciences.</note>

<margin>Frankfurt de Knebelbeck possesses me</margin> <note>This is a provenance note written by a former owner of the book, indicating it belonged to a member of the Knebelbeck family in Frankfurt.</note>

**A.** Greetings, Master.
**B.** And to you, my good man.
**A.** I am going to give you my son <note>The speaker is offering his son to the teacher for his education.</note>.
**B.** And I shall return him to you.
**A.** In what condition?
**B.** Both learned and successful.
**A.** These are excellent things, but I beg you, explain how.
**B.** From me, he will learn how to persuade men of whatever he wishes, how to track down the truth everywhere, to know all of Nature, to examine the heavens with precision, to shape his life perfectly, to govern citizens with wisdom, and to have God as an intimate friend.
**A.** I am stunned.
**B.** Why so?
**A.** Because you offer these things to others, yet you reserve none of them for yourself.
**A.** <note>The text repeats speaker A here, likely continuing the skeptical critique.</note> Nothing?
**B.** <note>Speaker B responds "Omnino," which can mean "entirely" or "absolutely," perhaps attempting to defend his total mastery before being interrupted.</note> Absolutely.
**A.** Not at all: for you do not persuade me of this, nor do you speak the truth, nor do you have Nature as a friend, nor the heavens favorable, nor a life approved by good men, nor obedient citizens, nor a merciful God.
**B.** This is an injustice!
**A.** On the contrary, it is a kindness, as I am judging you no more harshly than this: that you were going to trade mere words for money <note>original: "verba daturus eras pro ære"; a Latin idiom for selling empty promises or "selling air" for profit.</note>.

### THE CALLING. <note>original: "Vocatio." This refers to the formal summons to a church office or career.</note>

It is an outrage; you should have been called. **B.** Fool; if indeed I were willing to wait for another age to pass. **A.** So it is necessary to solicit the position? **B.** Rather, to buy it. For in such a crowd of candidates, if there had been money, I would not be grieving now. **A.** But what of the calling itself? **B.** That is owed to those who have the right of primogeniture <term>primogeniture: the legal right of the eldest son to inherit the entire estate or office</term>, or of inheritance. **A.** You speak obscurely. **B.** So it is fitting in the mysteries. **A.** So you lay down either a family name or silver as the foundation for the sacred office? **B.** Such are the demands of the times. **A.** And do you buy the care of souls <term>care of souls: "cura animarum," the spiritual responsibility of a priest for his congregation</term>? **B.** Are we not forced to? **A.** Do you sell them? **B.** If the hope of the wool is worth more. <note>A cynical metaphor: the priest values the "wool" (the income or tithes) more than the "sheep" (the people's souls).</note> **A.** Is there no conscience here? **B.** Poverty prevents it. **A.** Naturally, you are destined for priestly leisure <term>priestly leisure: "sacerdotale otium," a critical term for clergy who live off church wealth without performing labor</term> by your parents in such numbers that you ought to be kept away from the Church, not entreated to join. Hence, from the very first day you enter, you manage your own affairs, not His. **B.** Our own people must be fed. **A.** If indeed the care of the Church is a form of maintenance, or rather a way of growing rich, I shall no longer wonder if you devote yourself solely to this matter. **B.** Not solely, but after the sacred sermons have been delivered. **A.** What if that very sermon of yours should urge "sacred poverty"? **B.** One thing is appropriate for the pulpit <term>pulpit: "cathedra," literally the chair of authority from which a teacher or bishop speaks</term>, another for household management <term>household management: "oeconomia," the practical administration of one's private finances and home</term>. **A.** Or if it should commend generosity to men? **B.** If any—

## 4. MACHIAVELLI.

**A.** Why are you building a fire? 

**B.** Piety <note>original: "pietas." In this context, B is suggesting that burning "heretical" or "evil" books is an act of religious duty.</note> commands it. 

**A.** A fiery piety? 

**B.** A pestilential man must be destroyed. 

**A.** Who is he: is it Aristotle? <note>Aristotle's works were the foundation of medieval education, but were increasingly attacked by Renaissance and Reformation thinkers.</note> 

**B.** Even his words ought to be burned. 

**A.** Do as you please, but show me the accused. 

**B.** It is that Florentine scoundrel. 

**A.** Bah! Machiavelli, <term>Machiavelli</term> <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) was a diplomat and philosopher from Florence. His name became synonymous with ruthless pragmatism and the separation of politics from traditional morality.</note> a wretched and utterly foolish man. 

**B.** And yet he is the father of all the most crafty minds; I wish the earth had never produced him, or that the underworld had swallowed him the moment he was born. 

**A.** Are the things that fool wrote truly so unbearable? 

**B.** Exceedingly so; but why do you call him a fool? 

**A.** Because whatever great harms to republics and <term>secrets of state</term> <note>original: "arcana imperiorum." This term refers to the "mysteries" or hidden mechanisms of power that rulers use to maintain control.</note> he observed, he dared to make public—certainly to his own great infamy and the hatred of others. 

**B.** What? Is he not the author and advisor of wicked deeds? 

**A.** Not at all: rather, he is a traitor <note>A suggests Machiavelli is a "traitor" to the ruling class because he revealed their secret tactics to the public.</note> and far too candid, for he did not blush to say what others not only think, but firmly believe and practice throughout their whole lives. 

**B.** Why then does everyone detest the man? 

**A.** Justly so, for those who rule are pained to see their tricks uncovered...

**B.** Even among us? 

**A.** Absolutely: for to wish to be the most sincere of all in Christian profession and to agree with the Scriptures to the letter <note>original: "ad unguem" – literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for perfect precision or finishing</note>, yet be no better in one's morals—what else is this but to mock Christ shamefully? 

**B.** Mortals will never be without defects. 

**A.** Never indeed; but I ask you, consider for yourself what blasphemies, luxuries, lusts, vanities, robberies, iniquities, pleasures, and deceptions are publicly tolerated among us, or even nearly approved.

# APOSTASY.

**B.** Are there not severe laws against the wicked, and very frequent examples of punishments?

**A.** For the weak, certainly; but the more powerful are "punished" with commendations. <note>original: "elogiis puniuntur." This is a satirical remark: the elite receive praise or honorary citations rather than actual justice.</note>

**B.** But these men await Christ as their judge.

**A.** Excellent! You see then that in this "less than Christian" administration of public affairs <note>original: "rerum publicarum minùs Christiana administratione"</note>, our concerns must be left to God himself. He governs this era by His own will in such a way that it cannot bring harm to the godly.

**B.** In the meantime, what will be owed to the defenders of the truth?

**A.** Great praise—though it would only be truly complete if they showed the same spirit in *imitating* Christ as they do in *claiming* Him.

**B.** That will happen, I believe, if our age requires some trial.

**A.** On the contrary, Christ himself requires it. This is the only thing that will keep our religion sound and safe <note>original: "sartam tectamque" — a Latin legal idiom meaning "in good repair," literally "patched and roofed."</note> for us.

**B.** We shall hope so.

**A.** Let us rather act and try, lest we be said to have blindly signed on to this knowledge while living a profane life that expresses the opposite.

**B.** Oh, how happy then would be Harmony! <note>original: "Concordia"</note>

**A.** Happy indeed. And unless that happens, I fear no other religion for us, except having none at all.

## 6. *THE TUTOR.*

*A.* So, are you satisfied? 

*B.* I would be a fussy man indeed if I were to complain when such happiness is at hand. 

*A.* I commend your taking advantage of the opportunity, but do you believe it will last? 

*B.* All the signs point that way. 

*A.* Which signs? 

*B.* The humility, sincerity, generosity, modesty, diligence, and piety of the pupil—clearly the seeds of a hero who will one day rule for the welfare of the people. 

*A.* You speak of magnificent things, to which we rightly add our own prayers; meanwhile, I have my doubts. <note>original: "hæsito" — literally "I hesitate" or "I am stuck." A is skeptical of the tutor's optimism.</note>

*B.* In vain. His character is in my hands; like soft wax, it will be shaped by these fingers. 

*A.* By what arts, I ask? 

*B.* The most noble; indeed, by the very marrow of all Philosophy. For he will not be schooled according to the dry rules of grammarians, but most clearly by the refinements of nature. 

*A.* I pity you. 

*B.* Pity me? I, who am ready to help you and yours through my influence? <note>original: "interceſſione" — B implies that his position as the tutor to a future ruler gives him political leverage or "intercession" at court.</note>

*A.* You had better look out for your own old age right now; for unless I am very much mistaken, yours will be ignoble and wretched. 

*B.* You are talking nonsense. 

*A.* You do not realize that your "letters" <note>original: "literas" — referring to the tutor's scholarly teaching and humanist education.</note> are only tolerable for a very few years; your warnings will be merely excused, and your loyalty will not be considered of any great value. <note>original: "fidelitatē non capitalem" — A suggests the tutor's loyalty won't be the "capital" or primary concern of the prince once he grows up.</note>

*B.* I do not follow you. 

*A.* You will understand soon enough, when other masters succeed you who are far more popular—those whom Pallas <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom (Athena), representing the tutor's intellectual and moral education.</note> will not provide, but rather Jupiter, Mars, and Venus. <note>These Roman gods represent the worldly temptations of power (Jupiter), war (Mars), and carnal pleasure (Venus) which A predicts will eventually corrupt the student.</note>

*B.* You are an Oedipus. <note>A reference to the mythological figure who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; B is saying that A speaks in riddles or is acting as a cryptic prophet.</note> *A.*

## II. THE STRANGER TO THE WORLD.

<note>original title: "COSMOXENUS" — a Greek-derived term for someone who is a stranger or guest in the world</note>

### 13 THE LATIN LANGUAGE.

**A.** I have always tolerated the ambition of the Latin language, albeit with difficulty; but that it exercises tyranny over the Church <note>original: "Eccleſiam"</note>—that is too much.

<margin>A.</margin> What is this good fortune of our age, that from so many most wise writers and past centuries, the most perfect form of the State <term>Respublica: literally 'the public thing,' referring here to the commonwealth or the structured form of government</term> can be prescribed? *B.* That is surely to be wise at another's expense <note>original: "alieno damno" — a proverb suggesting learning from others' mistakes or using others' resources</note>. *A.* Especially; but to what height will the daring of our wits finally climb? *B.* To that point from where, spinning with dizziness, they may shamefully fall. *A.* Why, do you not favor this ingenious century, this learned age? *B.* In such a way, certainly, that I pity most men. *A.* Come, what is more fortunate than to look upon the entire cycle of the world and from there select what is most rare, most prudent, and most perfect? *B.* What is more beautiful than to decorate new houses with various shields bought in the market? *A.* What is more elegant than to organize legal and military matters according to the counsel of all antiquity? *B.* What is more fitting than to dress our little boys <note>original: "pusiones"</note> in our own oversized boots <note>original: "caligis" — heavy military or walking boots; B is using a metaphor to suggest ancient laws are too large and ill-fitting for the present</note>? *A.* I do not see what you are getting at. *B.* Namely, that the times do not match, and that God adds His own ornament to every scene, and gives to His own...

### 16. ACONTIUS.

**A.** What should I say is the reason that, while in all other matters men are most distrustful, they entrust their religion to <term>Doctors: "Doctoribus," meaning teachers of theology or high-ranking academics</term> with the greatest confidence? 

**B.** Because the assertion of our religious <term>leaders: "Antistitum," high-ranking clergy or overseers</term> is so consistent, and their refutation of the opposing side so powerful, that everyone considers it a <note>original: "piaculum" — a sin or an act requiring atonement</note> crime not to believe men of such gravity and composed expression—men who seem no less concerned for their own salvation than for yours, and who appear most fair in examining the foundations of the opposing side. 

**A.** Meanwhile, that which should have been examined by many—indeed, by almost everyone—is instead committed to one, or indeed to very few. 

**B.** Justly so: for not all are of such firm judgment that they may safely engage with the books of their adversaries. 

**A.** Yet would you wish the books of your own religion to be available to everyone and everywhere? 

**B.** One cannot hope for that, such is the hatred of the truth. 

**A.** And you wish for all the rest to be extinguished? 

**B.** At least that they be prohibited from the <note>original: "officinis," meaning workshops or bookshops</note> shops. 

**A.** And yet you condemn these books—neglected, unseen, and uncorrected—based on the judgment of another, which is often a rash judgment.

### 17. APOTHEOSIS.

**A.** What folly was it of the Romans, who believed that those who were men today should be worshipped as Gods tomorrow? 

**B.** Or rather, were they more foolish, or perhaps more wicked, who were ready to receive the living Alexander into the number of the Gods once a price had been accepted? <note>A reference to Alexander the Great’s demands for divine honors and the willingness of some Greek cities to grant them for political favor.</note> 

**A.** It is believable that none of them actually believed they were Gods, but were merely playing a trick on the ignorant. 

**B.** The same thought comes to my mind whenever I look upon the modern <term>apotheosis: "ἀποθέωσις," the process of elevating a human being to divine or saintly status</term>. 

**A.** The Antichristian one? <note>Likely referring to the Roman Catholic practice of canonizing saints, which Protestants of this era often labeled as "Antichristian."</note> 

**B.** Certainly; but also our own. For in almost as many funeral sermons as I observe, or eulogies for the dead, I seem to be able to count just as many new Gods. 

**A.** I, on the contrary, see there so many learned meditations on death and examples of a most praiseworthy life. 

**B.** For as many as leave behind enough money for a funeral...

# ### 19. HYPOCRITES.

<margin>A.</margin> ...physicians <note>original: "physicos" — the OCR begins mid-word from the previous page</note> to be wholesome, and lawyers to be just, and theologians to be religious; but now, what more do you wish me to do? **B.** To know for certain that the whole world is playing a part <note>original: "histrioniam" — referring to the theater or the life of an actor; a common Renaissance trope of the "world as a stage"</note>. **A.** It is apparent: for while all things present one appearance to the world, they actually seek another in truth. **B.** But avoid as diligently as possible those who possess more hypocrisy than others. **A.** Are there signs by which I might judge them? **B.** Scarcely enough, but let these be your general guides: a furrowed brow <note>original: "frons caperata" — a wrinkled forehead meant to convey false seriousness or deep piety</note>, a studied gait, long and flowing robes, affected speech, and a frequent railing against the vices of others. **A.** Are those things actually bad, or merely suspicious? **B.** Put it to the test: you will find them to be slanderous, grasping <note>original: "viscosos" — literally "sticky," implying people who latch onto others for their own benefit</note>, envious, and bloodthirsty, if they are given the chance. **A.** And yet, it should be easy to strip these wicked men of their mask of hypocrisy with a single example. **B.** You are mistaken; it is a multifaceted thing, and impossible to untangle because of its frequent twists and turns. **A.** I do not know what is coming to my mind. **B.** What is it then? ## 25. THE ACADEMY.

**A.** As many as have ever soared into the breeze of good fame seem to me to have been raised up on the wings of **Dialectic** <note>The art of logical investigation and argument.</note> and **Rhetoric** <note>The art of persuasive speaking or writing.</note>. 

**B.** You have named two of the best things, and two of the worst. 

**A.** You are quibbling over names; I mean the arts of discovering and persuading people of the truth. 

**B.** That sounds fair enough, but I do not want any others than those. 

**A.** Or are you hostile to the truth? 

**B.** Not at all, but to the <term>Lesbian rule</term> <note>original: "Lesbiæ regulæ." A "Lesbian rule" was a flexible leaden ruler used by masons on the island of Lesbos that could bend to fit the shape of a stone; metaphorically, it refers to a standard that is bent to suit one's own desires rather than following an absolute truth.</note>. 

**A.** Explain yourself. 

**B.** Naturally, it is suspect to me because, having abandoned Christian simplicity and the weight of the Divine Word, it successfully defends either side of an argument and persuades one of what is false with the same ease. 

**A.** Will you really doubt the most excellent arts? 

**B.** Indeed I will, and so **Dr. Luther** <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German reformer, who was often highly critical of "Scholastic" logic and the way it was used to complicate the simple message of the Bible.</note> taught me: for just as truth is evaded there by various petty distinctions and axioms, so here it is overwhelmed by a mass of words and seductive charms. 

**A.** And yet, no one of sound mind has ever disapproved of the investigation and the eloquent expression of the truth. 

**B.** Nor will it ever happen; the only thing that matters is by what rules the actual truth is established, and by what formulas it is declared. 

**A.** Surely by Academic rules: for who could possess them more exactly than those who spend their entire lives within them? 

**B.** I admit that these belong both to the Scholastic— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "corum" indicates the next word is "Scholasticorum" (of the Scholastics).</note>

## 27. PEDAGOGISM.

<margin>A.</margin> Why is it that schoolmasters <note>original: "literarum magistri." Literally "masters of letters."</note>, when brought forth to manage public affairs, are usually the most incompetent of all mortals? **B.** Because they sometimes focus their minds on such trivial things, even while they dwell upon the loftier contemplation of human affairs. **A.** But if anyone were to catch them in that very "citadel of contemplation," they would find them sweating over grammatical constructions, linguistic anomalies, and irregular words <note>original: "anomalis, & heteroclitis." ## 29. *THE TREASURY.*

**A.** What tablets <note>original: "tabellas"; referring to wax tablets or account books used for record-keeping</note> are you carrying here, I pray? **B.** They are accounts. **A.** You, a man of religion, keeping accounts? **B.** Indeed, sacred ones, for they belong to our treasury <term>aerarium: originally the public treasury of Rome, here used for a church or community fund</term>, or rather, the purse. **A.** The birdlime? <note>original: "Visci?"; a pun on the speaker's mention of "fisci" (the purse/fisc). I would wish my integrity to be clear to the world. **A.** From where does this sum of silver come? **B.** It is usually collected on feast days or Church solemnities from men of good will. **A.** For what use? **B.** For the almonry <note>original: "Eleemosynarium"; a fund specifically designated for the relief of the poor</note>. **A.** Let me run through it. **B.** Look at the totals instead. **A.** Very well.

To beggars: 3 fl. <term>fl.: florins, a gold or silver coin used throughout Europe</term>
To scholars: 10 bac. <term>bac.: batzen, a silver coin of modest value common in southern Germany and Switzerland</term>
To widows: 1 fl.
To the musicians <note>original: "Simphoniacis"; refers to the choir or instrumentalists providing music for liturgy</note>: 6 fl.
To the painter: 34 fl.
To the exiles: 2 fl.
To the cabinetmaker <note>original: "Scriniario"; an artisan who makes chests or shrines, or potentially a registrar</note>: 10 fl.
To the washerwoman: 20 bac.
For various restorations: 18 fl.
For banquets: 60 fl.

Ho there! Is this last item equally considered "Alms"? **B.** Why not? For since we are occupied the whole year in receiving and paying out coins, should we not be allowed to feast four times? **A.** More often, even; if you admit that you are "almsgiving guests." **B.** You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. <note>A quote from Deuteronomy 25:4, often used in the New Testament to justify the support of ministers</note> **A.** Take back the accounts; I fear I shall find more absurdities. **B.** On the contrary, you would have found our sacred temple and the houses of the ministers well-adorned this year—

## 32 *HERETICS.*

**A.** What injustice of nature is this, that falsehood is fertile, while truth is sterile? **B.** Why are you so upset? <note>original: *stomacharis*; literally "why is your stomach churning," a common Latin idiom for being annoyed or angry.</note> **A.** I am angry at the sects <term>sectis: religious or philosophical factions that have broken away from a main body</term>, which sprout forth in great numbers from a single trunk. **B.** Perhaps you believe there are as many sects as there are hateful names commonly tossed about? **A.** Certainly: for hardly is an ambitious mind born that does not strive for a following of error and disciples. **B.** You do not agree with me. **A.** But the multitude of sects is obvious. **B.** To be sure, there are names, but they seem to me to have been devised to create hatred rather than being sought after by the authors of any actual disagreement. **A.** At last, you will play the advocate for heretics! **B.** Yes: since the scope of that name is so broad that it can be cast upon even the most innocent person as easily as it is done by great consensus. **A.** Watch what you say; it is no light matter to excuse a heretic, and to defend one is even most dangerous. **B.** Once, indeed, the name of heresy was detestable to all pious people; now it is a matter of "theological generosity" <note>original: *Theologicæ liberalitatis*; here used sarcastically to mean that theologians throw the term "heretic" around far too freely and "generously."</note> to call someone a heretic. For today even a Simon Magus <term>Simon Magus: a biblical figure associated with sorcery and the sin of "simony" (buying church offices), here representing a corrupt or false religious authority</term> excommunicates the most sincere people, and a Machiavellian <note>original: *Macchianellus*; a reference to Niccolò Machiavelli, used here to describe a cynical, power-hungry person who uses religion as a tool.</note> proscribes good men, and— **A.** I beg you, do not even suspect such a thing.

## 35. THE WALDENSIANS.

**A.** What reason do you suspect lies beneath the fact that, while nearly all religions urge and insist upon holiness of life and integrity, they very rarely seem to achieve them?

**B.** Perhaps it happens because of the diversity of men; for one nation is more manageable, while another is more wild.

**A.** That is not enough; for you can see men of the most diverse nations, on account of the profession of a single religion, agree closely in their morals and pursuits. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, every religion brings its own way of living with it, as it were.

**B.** In the case of the Papists <note>original: *pontificijs* — a common early modern term for Roman Catholics</note> and the Anabaptists, the reason is evident: for them, piety is mercenary <note>This suggests their good behavior is motivated by the hope of "buying" salvation or earning merit.</note>.

**A.** Meanwhile, do you acknowledge that something can be present in a religion which more easily entices one toward integrity?

**B.** It appears so.

**A.** What then do you think is lacking in our most sincere <note>The speaker likely refers to the Reformed or Protestant tradition they belong to.</note> faith, which indeed strongly urges piety, yet obtains nothing, or very little at all?

**B.** If one may venture a guess, I would believe that the dealings of religion and the State <note>original: *Reipubl.* — shorthand for *Respublica*</note> are too much against di- <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword *stinctas* indicates the next word is *distinctas* (distinct or separated).</note>

"All men," (says a Catholic writer <note>original: *Pontificius* — likely an inquisitor or hostile historian whose records provide the description</note>) "and women, small and great, by night and by day, do not cease to learn and to teach; for the laborer in..."

**A.** You have almost moved me to tears; for what are we doing in such great light of the Gospel?

**B.** Oh, if only we would join doctrine and life together! Now, if their doctrine condemns others, and their life condemns us, who, I ask, will be saved?

## 38. PRAYERS.

*A.* Among so many books of prayer, both ancient and recent, which one would you wish to be most familiar to me? 

*B.* What are you thinking of? The one which necessity—the most eloquent and ingenious of all things—has created. 

*A.* Who is that author? What trifles are you talking about? 

*B.* I speak seriously: I believe no formula is more perfect than that which the Cross of Christ <note>original: *Crux Christi*</note> has dictated.

*B.* Do you suppose that flattering words and a structure of language recited from a sheet can persuade God of anything?

*B.* Does the Lord’s Prayer <term>dominica oratio; the "Our Father," considered by Christians to be the model for all prayer</term> not suffice for you—to which not even the whole world could add or subtract anything? ## BOASTING.

The possessions of philosophers <note>original: *Philosophorum possessiones*; referring to intellectual and spiritual wealth rather than material goods</note> are of such a kind that, having been raised by them to the heights, they look down upon you—the guardians of metals and the diggers of the earth—laughing at you with a sweet contempt. 

*A.* Are you speaking of those men? The ones whom the wealthy hire for the lowest price, through whose tongues they tell their lies, on whose shoulders they are lifted up, by whose fantasies they are delighted, by whose deaths they live, and whom they kill with a harsh gaze? 

*B.* No, rather I speak of those who rule over the stars, who partition the earth, who shape human character, who challenge nature, laugh at fortune, trample upon riches, soar through the heavens with their intellect <term>ingenio; natural talent or genius</term>, rebuke tyrants, and hold death as a familiar companion. 

*A.* Bah! You are always setting those ancient Heroes—mere dreams and shadows of the wise—against us; they are nothing but bugbears to frighten children <note>original: *puerorum terriculamenta*; literally "things used to terrify boys"</note>. I, however, reproach you with modern examples, who are scarcely even mimics of the ancients: specifically, those whom the characters of a calendar <note>original: *Calendarii characteres*; likely referring to an obsession with astrology or the anxieties of keeping a schedule</note> torture, or whom the acreage of a small field puffs up with pride, or whom the little commotions of a wife drive in circles, or whom the common admiration for their craft carries away, or whom a chance accident casts down, or whom the hope of a small coin spurs on, or whom filthy bonds restrain, or whom the whims of Princes drag along with them, or whom the memory of death strikes breathless. 

Meanwhile, the names of Lycurgus, Plato, Aristotle, Pliny, Euclid, Galen, Livy, Vir- <note>original: *Lycurgi, Plat. Arist. Plin. Eucl. Gal. Liv. Vir...*; a list of foundational Greek and Roman authors in law, philosophy, science, and literature</note>

<header>CONVERSATION.</header>

To me indeed, it is most sweet to have learned through long experience and intimate conversation that those men are no better or more certain of things than others, but are instead more slippery and talkative.

## 40. CONVERSATION.

**A.** How unfair is my lot, that I have never been admitted among the weightier discussions and most prudent consultations of those men upon whom the whole state and the <term>republic of letters; the international community of scholars and intellectuals</term> rest? 

**B.** Why do you adopt such a tragic tone here? 

**A.** What else can I bring, but the seething of my thoughts? Because they have nowhere been examined by the censures <note>original: *censuris*; referring here to critical judgment or official review</note> of the most Excellent men, they have never been settled or subdued. Instead, they riot among themselves in the shadows of poverty and obscurity, while you most fortunate ones possess the decisions on all matters through a great shortcut. You either decently educate and polish the offspring of your genius <note>original: *ingenij fœtus*; a common metaphor in this period comparing intellectual ideas to newborn children</note> as soon as they are born, according to the most exact judgments of your "Approved" men, or you suffocate them <note>i.e., suppress ideas that do not meet the standard</note> with total security. 

**B.** Does nature teach you nothing, or does the innate fruitfulness of your talent draw out nothing, or does your frequent reading not educate you, such that you must run to living reciters and interpreters of the most obvious things? 

**A.** It appears you are unaware...

## 41. THE BANQUET.

*B.* Let them be so, but please, recount the order of the banquet.

## 48. PRAISE OF NERO.
<note>original: *Neronis Encomium*; an "encomium" is a formal speech or piece of writing that highly praises someone or something, often used as a rhetorical exercise to defend the indefensible.</note>

...you might understand, Nero has never been excused, but rather compared with those whom the World <note>original: *Mundus*; often used in a theological sense to mean the secular or ungodly world</note> believes to be most innocent. We do this so that we might learn, through such great artistry, that Nero was not the only tyrant; rather, there were many before and after him—and indeed, there are very many even today, if anyone were willing to examine the matter with a fair scale and judge with a free tongue. From this, our Christianity uniquely and everywhere instills the fear and reverence of God, as well as a spirit of harmony <note>original: *consensum*; implying a shared agreement or moral alignment</note>, so that those placed in charge of others do not rule by their own whim <note>original: *suô arbitriô*; referring to absolute or arbitrary will without legal or moral restraint</note>, but instead refer all things to the laws of Heaven. Once this sense of duty is lost or weakened, monsters and crimes against humanity immediately spring forth to afflict the world. 

Because a certain noble writer <note>This likely refers to Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), whose *Encomium Neronis* was a famous example of "paradoxical encomium"—praising a subject generally considered beyond defense to sharpen one's rhetorical skills or deliver a veiled critique of current rulers.</note> had known and experienced such things in his own time, he did not want posterity to be so deceived by foul flattery <note>original: *turpi adulatione*</note> that they would worship as Gods or saving Deities <note>original: *salutaribus Numinibus*; "Numen" refers to a divine power or spirit</note> those who had scarcely deserved even a beastly name among men. ### 49. FABLES.

**A.** I am often inclined to be angry with historians who have dared to hawk the most fantastical fables as truths, as if those who come after us would possess no judgment of their own.

## 54. THE TRIUMPH OF VANITY.

**A.** Is it also permitted to recount dreams? 

**B.** To recount them is permitted, but to despise them is proper. 

**A.** Yet it is pleasant to be happy, even while sleeping. 

**B.** Do you not know how often gold is wont to turn into dung? <note>A proverbial warning against the deceptive nature of dreams or worldly riches; what appears as treasure in a dream is often revealed as filth upon waking.</note> 

**A.** Listen, nevertheless, then judge as it seems best. 

**B.** Recount it then, dreamer. 

**A.** At that time, when we were dancing everywhere with insolent joy, I saw **Vanity Triumphant**. <note>original: *Triumphantem Vanitatem*; "Vanity" here refers to the biblical concept of *Vanitas*—the fleeting, empty, and futile nature of worldly pursuits.</note>

**B.** What wonder is there in that? Since we see it daily, and we do so while groaning. 

**A.** But this vision of mine was consistent in all its parts. 

**B.** You seem to have seen something entirely emptier than vanity itself: tell us then. 

**A.** First, **Talkativeness** came forward with a trumpet, intended to call together the spectators in the place of Fame, I suppose; both painting and the printing press <note>original: *prælum*; the author suggests that art and published books are the servants of empty chatter and self-promotion.</note> served as her handmaidens. 

**B.** A sufficiently worthy beginning. 

**A.** Then, with great weariness, two most scrawny little horses followed, called **Labor** and **Fidelity**. 

**B.** Alas, for our lot! 

**A.** Two charioteers were placed upon them: **Idleness** and **Overindulgence**. <note>original: *Crapula*; specifically refers to the intoxication or the sick-headache and lethargy resulting from excessive drinking and eating.</note>

**B.** Ah, what an unjust lot! 

**A.** There were also added two figures goading them on: **Flattery** and **Custom**. 

**B.** Troublesome... <note>The Latin text ends mid-sentence with the word *Importunæ*; the catchword "tunæ" suggests the next page begins with "fortunæ," likely meaning "Troublesome [goads of] fortune."</note>

### 61. *THE ONE WHO WAITS.*

**A.** **W**hat do those bandages around your neck mean? ...beats me back, the wheel <note>A reference to the *Rota Fortunae* or Wheel of Fortune, a common medieval and Renaissance concept where some are raised to the top of the wheel while others are crushed at the bottom.</note> moves forward, and those whom I had already nearly won over, it lifts even higher, and then it throws new people in my path. <margin>65.</margin>## MOROPROTEREMA
<note>The title is a Greek-derived term combining 'moros' (fool) and 'proterema' (advantage or success), which translates to "The Fool's Advantage" or "Foolish Preeminence."</note>

<margin>A.</margin>**W**hat are you laughing at? **B.** At ridiculous people. **A.** Then you are laughing at yourself. **B.** And at you as well, unless you laugh along with me. **A.** A great force of fools you have there. **B.** On the contrary, a partnership. This one wanted the **fingers of Midas** <note>The King whose touch turned everything to gold</note>, that one the **ring of Gyges** <note>A mythical ring that granted invisibility</note>, another the **hair of Sambron** <note>Likely a reference to a legendary figure known for strength or beauty, common in Renaissance lists of impossible gifts</note>, another the **lyre of Orpheus** <note>Which could charm animals and stones</note>, someone else the **wings of Daedalus**, another the **Gorgon of Perseus** <note>The head of Medusa, used to turn enemies to stone</note>, someone the **purse of Fortunatus** <note>A legendary pouch that was never empty of gold</note>, several the **tongue of Mithridates** <note>King Mithridates VI was famously said to be able to speak twenty-two different languages</note>, and even one who wanted the **incantations of Zoroaster** <note>original: "preculas" — literally "little prayers," here referring to the magical spells attributed to the ancient Persian sage</note>, and right next to him, the **laughter of Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata, a famous Greek satirist who mocked human vanity and religion</note>. **A.** And were you silent? **B.** It did occur to me to laugh sweetly on behalf of everyone who made a wish; but that was not permitted among men of such "solemn beards" <note>original: "promissae barbae" — long beards were often a sign of a philosopher, here used to imply they were trying to look more serious than they were</note>. Therefore, I sought one thing, and the most noble: **The Fool's Advantage** <note>original: μωροπροτέρημα (moroproterema)</note>.

<header>TRUTH.</header>

...truth can be expressed in various ways, depending on how the mind is predisposed. For if some wished to call us fools, it would undoubtedly be true, but each person would understand it in a different way. **A.** See if you can, if you please, make me out to be a fool multiple times, and in different ways? **B.** Very easily—both in a malicious sense and in a good one. **A.** Let us hear it. **B.** Consider if some Julian <note>original: *Julianus*; referring to Julian the Apostate (331–363 AD), the Roman Emperor who renounced Christianity and mocked Christians for prioritizing the afterlife over the present</note> calls you a fool because you neglect the present life for the sake of the future. You accept this title, which Paul <note>original: *Paulus*; referring to the Apostle Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians 4:10: "We are fools for Christ's sake"</note> says is honorable and precious to God. Did not the former speak the truth impiously, and the latter piously? Now, if some haughty person reproaches you for your lack of worldly goods, and a Christian celebrates your poverty, both have spoken the truth; they have described an "earthly fool," but with very different intentions. Furthermore, if someone envious notes a defect in your talent, while a fair-minded man modestly warns you of your faults, you have once again been made a fool twice over, by two different tellers of truth. Finally, if some buffoon shamefully mocks you, and another witty person sharply critiques you, you will be a fool according to both a bitter truth and a clever one. I say no more. For it is enough to show that truth can be impious <note>original: *veritatem... impiam*</note>, such as Satan’s truth when he confronts sinners <note>In Christian theology, Satan is the "Accuser" who speaks the truth about a person's sins, but does so to cause despair rather than repentance</note>, or it can be pious <note>original: *piam*</note>, such as the Church’s truth whenever she calls back those who go astray; or another...

<header>TRUTH.</header>

...illicit <note>original: *licitam*; completing the word "illicitam" from the previous page's catchword. In this context, it refers to an unauthorized or unrestrained way of speaking the truth</note>, such as that of the mockers, the carping critics <note>original: *zoilorum*; referring to Zoilus, a Greek grammarian known for his bitter and pedantic attacks on Homer</note>, and the fanatics, who take sole delight in the errors of men; another is humane, such as that of those who devote their labors and most skillful investigations to the commonwealth; another is puffed up, such as the Aristotelian <term>Aristotelian: referring to the followers of Aristotle, who were often criticized by Renaissance humanists for being overly argumentative and obsessed with intellectual dominance</term>, which fights against all opinions and strives for mastery; another is modest, such as that of Christians, by whom revealed truths are guarded with simple faith and spread with a humble voice; another is biting, such as the Diogenic <term>Diogenic: following the style of Diogenes the Cynic, who used blunt, harsh truth-telling to shame others and challenge social norms</term>, which finds pleasure in pure rebukes and the most bitter words; another is festive, such as the Socratic <term>Socratic: referring to the irony of Socrates, who used humor and indirect questioning to lead others to wisdom</term>, which gradually sways people with its bright wit <note>original: *candido sale*; literally "white salt," a common Latin idiom for elegant or refined wit</note> and leads them, almost without their knowing and while they are focused on other things, toward serious and good matters. *A.* Indeed, you have now led me to believe it. For no statement is truer than that we are all fools.

The speaker is making a pun: "I greet you, but you look like you need health/salvation."</note>. **B.** I pray that you yourself are sane and capable of health. **A.** What kind of monster is this? ## 74. THE DEGREE.

*A.* Greetings, Lord Master. *B.* Good words to you. *A.* Forgive me if some higher degree has fallen to you; I remember that you were a Master <note>original: *Magister*; the standard academic title for one who had completed the liberal arts curriculum</note>. *A.* On the contrary, you reproach me for an injury done to me. *B.* An injury, truly? *A.* Why not? Since I, a fool, was buying what did not exist, was nothing, and was nowhere. *B.* You speak of monstrous things. *A.* And the peddlers <note>original: *institores*; refers here to university officials or those selling academic credentials</note> sold me what they could not give, did not have, and did not want to provide. *B.* You should have bought hellebore <note>original: *Helleborum*; a plant used in antiquity as a remedy for madness; B is suggesting that A was insane to pay for such a title</note>. *A.* I would rather have bought that than that smoke <note>original: *fumum*; a common metaphor for something empty, vain, or non-existent</note>. *A.* Tell me if anything absurd has happened to you. *B.* You say this well. For I allowed myself to be persuaded that I knew what I did not know, and that I was what I was not—and never will be—and to rejoice and accept congratulations for a thing of nothing. *B.* That is, to boast of being full while starving, and to pay the bill <note>original: *symbolum*; a contribution or a share of the cost for a meal or event</note>. *A.* And that is quite apt: for that persuasion cost me no small amount. For when I spent about thirty florins <note>original: *florenos*; high-value gold coins</note>, I learned it was easier to declare myself learned and skilled in the arts...

## 81. FORTIFICATION.

**A.** Is it permitted to look into these papers? **B.** To no one, except the most secret friend. **A.** Even if I were made of stone <note>meaning: "even if I were as silent as a statue"</note>, if you wish; for your secrets not even the torture-cords <note>original: *fidiculae*; small cords used to wring confessions from a witness</note> would wring from me. **B.** You speak boldly, but look: let this be granted to your loyalty and proven sincerity. **A.** And yet I see nothing but lines. **B.** Are you not skilled in these drawings? **A.** Not at all; therefore, take back these mysteries of yours. **B.** You must be informed: you see here the <term>ground plan</term> <note>original: *ignographia*; a horizontal map of a building's foundations</note> of some structure, then the <term>cross-section</term> <note>original: *sciographia*; a drawing showing the interior profile or "cutting through" of a building</term>, and finally the <term>elevation</term> <note>original: *orthographia*; a formal drawing of the front or side view</note>. **A.** I see them, but with eyes that are less than artistic <note>original: *minus graphicis*; meaning eyes untrained in technical drafting</note>. **B.** Does it not truly appear to be a most fortified castle <note>original: *castrum*</note>? ## 84. WRITERS.

**A.** Write, if you are writing anything. **B.** I do not know why my pen feels so sluggish <note>original: *stupeat*; literally "is stunned" or "numb"</note>. **A.** To you alone, perhaps? Especially in this "scribbling age," where even eunuchs beget children and the sterile give birth <note>A satirical jab at the explosion of printed books in the 17th century, implying that even those with no talent or "seed" are producing volumes of work.</note>. **B.** All the more reason to bite one's nails <note>original: *ungues rodendi*; a common Latin idiom for working painstakingly or anxiously over a piece of writing</note>, lest some monster be produced that ought to be banished from Sparta <note>Referring to the ancient Spartan custom of "exposure," where weak or deformed infants were cast out or abandoned.</note>. **A.** Here is the only precaution: write nothing serious. For seriousness is both suspected and hated by this current age—or indeed, looked upon as ridiculous. No one today gains the reputation of a "fanatic" more easily than the man who suggests caring for the soul in this brief summary of life <note>original: *breviario*; implying that life is a short manual or compendium</note>, or who advises one to embrace the fellowship of Christ, to utterly disregard the world, and to walk against its current. **B.** I do not know how serious I am. Certainly, I sometimes move myself to laughter, however bitter it may be; yet it is of no small importance how I might appear to others. **A.** Regarding the honest, the noble, the learned, and the wise, I tell you to be at ease. Such wit never offends them; rather, it sharpens and stimulates them. But as for the Anathematizers <note>Those who are quick to pronounce religious curses or formal condemnations</note> and the "Scrap-mongers"... <note>original: *Offariis*; likely referring to critics who hunt for small "scraps" or trifles to find fault with.</note>

## 85. APOLOGUE. <note>An "apologue" is a moral fable, often using animals as characters to comment on human behavior.</note>

<margin>A.</margin> **A**: I was coming to see you. 
**B**: I am glad to hear it, but what are you carrying? 
**A**: A mystical figure. 
**B**: It was just the same with Conrad <note>likely referring to Conrad Lycosthenes (1518–1561), famous for his encyclopedia of omens and prodigies, or perhaps Conrad Gesner.</note>, who fascinated the world with such things. 
**A**: And yet, they say that something of yours like this once leaked out somewhere. 
**B**: Ha ha ha! What generous credulity! But what, finally, are you bringing? 
**A**: Here—images that are, in my judgment, purely hieroglyphic. 
**B**: Have you not compared them at all with the works of the Joachimites <note>Followers of Joachim of Fiore, known for complex symbolic diagrams of history.</note>, or the Paracelsians <note>Followers of the alchemist Paracelsus, who used many cryptic symbols.</note>, or those of Lichtenberger <note>Johannes Lichtenberger, a popular 15th-century astrologer and prophet.</note>, or Bridget <note>St. Bridget of Sweden, famous for her published prophetic visions.</note>, or Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander, a Swiss scholar of secret meanings and linguistics.</note>, or the Strasbourgeois, with which our friend Wolfius <note>Johannes Wolf (1537–1600), author of a massive collection of "memorable and secret" portents and histories.</note> is so full? 
**A**: I did, but in vain; for they do not match at all. 
**B**: Bah! How simple you are. Don’t you know that whatever this is, it is the image of a Fable? 
**A**: A Fable, you say? But one that neither Aesop nor Ochinus <note>Bernardino Ochino (1487–1564), an Italian reformer who wrote satirical and theological dialogues.</note> ever devised. 
**B**: I certainly remember reading it somewhere. 
**A**: Recite it, if you please, and bring a torch <note>original: *facem*; a metaphor for providing clarity or illumination.</note> to this figure. 
**B**: It is a playful tale. Once an eagle was sick, bleary-eyed either from old age or from gluttony. A doctor was sought, and a crow, who boasted of a "Panacea" <note>original: *Panacen*; a legendary universal cure-all.</note>, readily appeared. Having prescribed a diet, he fed the eagle on chaff for a long time; but in the meantime—as if it were part of the agreement—he plucked out quite a few of its most prominent feathers.

### APOLOGUE. <note>A moral fable or allegory, often using animal characters to critique human society.</note>

By chance, a squawking **goose** <note>In allegories, the goose often represents a noisy, foolish, or low-born person.</note> arrived and accused the **raven** of trickery; it received some applause, but it ended its loyalty in a foul death. Finally, the **swan**, repeating the accusation against the raven, obtained the care of the **eagle** <note>The eagle typically represents the Emperor or a high sovereign power.</note> by a great consensus. By removing the chaff and applying **manna** <note>A miraculous food or, in alchemical terms, a pure medicine.</note>, the swan certainly restored no small amount of light to the eagle. 

However, a **bat**, also boasting of being a doctor, attempted a deed clearly like that of **Medea** <note>A reference to the myth where Medea tricked the daughters of Pelias into killing and boiling their father under the false promise of "regenerating" his youth.</note>, intending the eagle's death while boasting that it was to be regenerated. Only with difficulty, and not without wounds to the eagle, was the bat finally restrained. On another side, a too-wise **jackdaw** <note>The jackdaw often represents a pretentious person who mimics others.</note> looked down upon the raw manna and suggested **distillations** <note>Refining substances through heat, a core process in chemistry and alchemy.</note>, which were indeed approved by the votes of many and mixed with the swan’s medicines. 

Thus, while these physicians disagreed among themselves, the left eye was entrusted to one and the right to the other; as judgment was provoked on both sides, a strange confusion arose among the spectators. For the doctors did not lack talkativeness, nor was the eagle himself consistent, nor was applause denied to either side. But most of all, the **Cicada** <note>A cricket or locust, representing a persistent and empty talker.</note> chirped whatever came into its mouth <note>original: "quicquid in buccam venisset" — a Latin idiom for speaking without thinking.</note>, and filled the ears of everyone with a discordant noise and thoroughly contradictory trifles. Among these things, the eagle’s strength also...

<summary>A satirical fable depicting an eagle (a ruler) being treated by various birds (advisors or doctors) whose conflicting methods and pretension lead to chaos rather than a cure.</summary>

## 87. *THE POLYMATH.* <note>The title "Polimathes" refers to a person of wide-ranging knowledge or a "polymath."</note>

<margin>A.</margin> **A.** Throw the book away. 
**B.** I would prefer it to gold. 
**A.** At least set it down for a friend's sake. 
**B.** I do even that with difficulty: for to no one are good little books closer friends, or more reliable ones. 
**A.** That is the voice of an ox, not a man. I would even prefer oxen to those measly booklets. 
**B.** To the pigsty with you; the altar <note>original: "ara." Here, B likely refers to his study or desk as a sacred space of devotion, contrasting it with the "hara" or pigsty he assigns to the unlearned A.</note> shall be my concern. 
**A.** What then are these "human" pursuits of yours? 
**B.** Look, here is Mornay <note>Philippe de Mornay (1549–1623), a prominent French Protestant writer and statesman known as the "Huguenot Pope" for his immense learning and defense of the faith.</note>, a notable star of modern erudition. 
**A.** Has he accomplished anything else besides trying to persuade us of what we all already believe? 
**B.** Oh, that "credulous" faith of yours—or rather, your complacency! You who snore in the midst of Jews, Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici." A common term in this period for non-Christian people or classical philosophers.</note>, Philosophers, Atheists, Muslims <note>original: "Mahumethani."</note>, Antichristians, Barbarians, and fanatics—as if you were in some ship, to be carried into the heavens without any effort or rowing of your own. What could be imagined more reckless? But Mornay, when he first wished to establish the truth of Christianity <note>Referring to Mornay’s famous 1581 work *De la vérité de la religion chrétienne* (On the Truth of the Christian Religion).</note>, and then to reveal the mystery of iniquity <note>Referring to Mornay’s *Le Mystère d'iniquité* (1611), a history of the Papacy.</note>, what author did he not consult? What learning, eloquence, and sagacity did he not employ? We are left nearly stunned by his citations alone, let alone the sheer variety of matters...

## 89. NOBODY AND EVERYONE.

...[to be reve]red, or rather <insert>Hard Court</insert> <note>original: "Hof hart"</note>, because there you obtain what you desire only with hardship and difficulty. **A.** These are trivial things. **B.** I admit it, if you overlook their sharp wit; but I was delighted by this: that he provides a proper explanation for what they call <term>vobissation</term> <note>From the Latin "vos" (you, plural). This refers to the practice of addressing a single person in the plural, similar to the "royal we."</note> in the decrees of **Princes**. **A.** But does not their supreme dignity and excellence require that they be addressed differently than we "singular little animals" are addressed? **B.** You are mistaken if you believe that. Instead, by adopting the **Plural number**, they are not ashamed to issue a confession that counsel has been sought and consensus heard. Therefore, whenever you hear **"We, by the grace of God,"** <note>original: "nos Dei gratia"</note> you should always understand that there is an underlying, unanimous judgment of the wisest men and the <term>guardians of the state</term> <note>original: "Patriæ curatorum"</note>. B argues that addressing a prince as "you" (plural) implies he cannot act without others, which might be taken as an insult to his personal authority in certain contexts.</note>...

It concludes by suggesting that, conversely, subjects should address a prince in the singular to respect his individual authority.</summary>

### 94. *THE COMMON PEOPLE.*

<margin>A.</margin> **A**las, it is never right for anyone to trust the unfaithful crowd! <note>original: "Heu nihil infidæ fas quemquam fidere turbæ!" — a poetic lament on the instability of public opinion.</note> **B.** O, truths truer than true! Indeed, there is no merit that cannot be scattered by a slight breeze from another direction. Regarding this matter, not just any common souls, but the highest intellects—esteemed by both the **Great Men** <note>original: "Magnatibus" — high-ranking nobles or leaders.</note> and the people—stand as witnesses everywhere: For...

<margin>4. A.</margin> I suppose you have seen the Roman Triad? <note>The "Roman Triad" (Trias Romana) was a popular polemical theme in the 16th and 17th centuries, often used by critics to group together three "vices" or "errors" they associated with the Church of Rome.</note>

## 99. THE CLOCK.

<margin>A.</margin> **A.** Why is my observer yawning? *B.* Truly, a pleasant sight has been presented to me. *A.* As if you have never seen a clock before? *B.* Never, so far as I know, with these eyes: for as soon as I saw here the division of the day, the movements of the planets, the sequence of the little bells, and the balances of the wheels <term>librationes rotarum: the rhythmic swinging or oscillation of the clock’s internal mechanisms, like the escapement</term>, I turned my eyes inward. I looked upon the clock of this vast universe, whose motions are just as regular, as are the cycles of the wheels, the divisions of the Great Day, the indicators, and the hourly bells. *A.* That is easier said than explained. For even if I grant you the most secret division of time, and the regulated succession of the Monarchies <note>The "Four Monarchies" was a traditional way of dividing human history into four great empires (usually Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome) based on the Book of Daniel.</note>, and especially the admirable little wheels of the Church and the notable signs of the times, who would yet dare to define those great hours? Or what lynx-eyed <note>original: "lynceus," referring to Lynceus of Argos, an Argonaut famous for his sharp sight</note> person could discern this hourly table? For just as unskilled eyes look in vain upon sciotheric lines <term>lineas sciotericas: the hour-lines on a sundial that track the movement of a shadow</term> and perceive confusion rather than an image of the heavens, so it is whenever we contemplate those Divine lines depicted with various strokes upon the earthly wall; they are by no means in vain...

### 100. JESUS.

**S**ince there are two most distinguished hallmarks <note>original: "puncta," literally "points" or "features"</note> of Jesus Christ—a most wise doctrine and a most perfect life—and he entrusted both to his Church to be spread abroad: Why is it that so many are strenuously occupied with the former, going forth to defend Christian truth, while the latter is clearly neglected and lies hidden, as if buried under the customs of the world? For although Christians believe differently than the rest of the world, they do not, however, live differently.

From this, it happens quite often that one suspects we do not even know Christ sufficiently...

# THE MISER. I. <note>original: *AVARUS*</note>

## RASPINUS, HERACLITUS.

<margin>R.</margin> **Y**ou have said it well: these times are troublesome and most difficult, and it is not easy to keep one's head above water <note>original: *emergere*, literally "to emerge" or "to surface," used here in a financial or social sense</note>. H: Ah, I believe it has always been thus; I do not see more evil, only a different kind. R: I shall make you see it. First, know that all things are expensive to buy: wine, meat, bread, the labor of craftsmen <note>original: *artificum operas*</note>, even down to plots of land, houses, and furniture. H: What of it? R: Then, consider that men are prone to pleasures and luxury, wasteful of themselves, their wealth, and their time. H: Badly, as always. R: Furthermore, the craftsmen are plotters for money and hunters of unwary women <note>original: *muliercularum*, a diminutive often used patronizingly to imply vulnerability or lack of judgment</note>; they always have means to provoke buyers out of fools. H: Ah, an ancient evil. R: For this reason my father, who lived in a still simple and good age, lived more comfortably and happily on half of my current possessions. H: Is that so? R: Indeed. Moreover, all things made then—cloth, leather, indeed all utensils—were made more durable. Now, due to French influence <note>original: *ex Gallica introductione*, literally "from the French introduction," referring to the contemporary perception of French fashions as flimsy or overly refined compared to traditional goods</note>, everything is delicate and fragile. Behold—

<margin>R.</margin> Here are my father’s boots, my grandfather’s cap, and my great-grandfather’s small sword; ah, this is how one ought to follow in the footsteps of one's ancestors. <margin>H.</margin> Ah. <margin>R.</margin> Why do you sigh? The dialogue concludes with Raspinus’s ironic anxiety about death: he toils miserably only so his heirs might live in the very idleness he despises.</summary>

Oh, if only we endured as much for the sake of God or virtue as this man endures as a "martyr" <note>original: *martyrii* — Democritus uses the term ironically here to describe the self-inflicted suffering of the alcoholic compared to religious devotion.</note>, we would have surely progressed far in seeking and acquiring the good! The world is incorrigible, and there is no greater madman than he who tries to apply a remedy; "each of us suffers his own ghost" <note>original: *quisq; suas patimur manes* — A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.743), suggesting that each person must bear the consequences of their own soul's state or their individual destiny.</note>. Oh, the vain and ridiculous boasting of man regarding his monarchy over the world and the empire of reason! Let me depart from here lest I see even more ridiculous things. Ha ha he!

...I claim for myself as my own: a house, a city, a field, and everything. Then, since men nowhere tolerate or admit the truth, I rebuke and laugh at the great men and <term>Monarchs</term>; I accuse them of lying, vanity, fickleness, and treachery. Furthermore, while the rest of men are each intent on their own business and torment themselves most laboriously in them, I walk about securely, and I assess and examine the labors of individuals, and compare them with the rest of the human multitude. Afterward, because I know nothing, it appears that I know everything; or because I am ignorant of everything, I err less in knowledge <note>original: *scientia*. **B.** Sometimes to entice them with pleasures. **D.** That is pleasing. **B.** Sometimes to lead them around with trifles. **D.** What will be the result at last? **B.** That we may live comfortably and pleasantly among the fools. **D.** How many types of fools do you have, then? **B.** As many as the types of hats you will see <note>original: *pileorum genera*. In the early modern era, hats were distinct markers of social rank, profession, and character. Buratin suggests that every social "uniform" is merely a different style of fool's cap.</note>. **D.** Ha ha he. **B.** Hey you, I have something to say to these people, so leave. **D.** Gladly; for I also have things to do at home. **B.** Then good day. **D.** Then my thanks to you. **B.** Then go. **D.** Then farewell. **B.** Then be well. **D.** Then be a good man.

**B.** Fellow citizens, good men, wherever you are! If there is anyone who holds a <term>vexatious privilege</term> <note>original: *vexatorium... privilegium*. Likely referring to a legal exemption or a social right that allows one to annoy or harass others without consequence.</note>, or who firmly believes in his heart that he is not a fool, and knows <term>epistemically</term> <note>original: *Epistimonice*. Derived from the Greek *episteme* (knowledge); to know something with scientific or philosophical certainty rather than mere opinion.</note> that he is truly wise, let him step over to this side and abandon the rest of the foolish rabble. But as for us, if there is anything witty, biting, or insulting to be said, we shall turn away from those people so they do not hear, and speak it to the fools. And then the wise will see us from behind. But if something wise and learned is to be brought forward, we shall turn our faces to the wise, and the fools will see us <note>original: *à culo*. Literally "from the backside" or "from the arse."</note> from the rear. Such is the decree of the <term>Senate of the Morosophs</term> <note>original: *Morosophūm*. A "Morosoph" is a "wise fool," a common literary paradox in Renaissance humanism (most famously in Erasmus's *Praise of Folly*) describing someone who is foolish in the eyes of the world but wise in truth, or vice-versa.</note>. Furthermore, why are the study of **agriculture** and the knowledge of **mines** <note>original: *fodinarum*</note>—which were held in great honor among the ancients and have today been brought back to light through excellent books—scorned by students and left discarded?
