*Curio:* Therefore, is your **<term>Magic</term>** <note>The teacher is redefining magic not as sorcery, but as "polymathy"—the mastery of many different sciences and arts.</note> nothing else? 

*C.:* I call the Trinity to witness that it is nothing else than the study of many arts, and a diligent one at that. 

*Curio:* And why was there need for those solemn oaths and my devotions? 

*C.:* You understand those four precepts, and the **theatrical staging**. <note>original: *scenicum apparatum*; the teacher admits that the dramatic rituals were merely a "show" to impress or distract the public.</note> 

*Curio:* Indeed. 

*C.:* Ha ha he! That is how I am accustomed to receive all curious seekers; I prefer that they retain this [mysterious] opinion of me and leave me to myself, rather than disturb me with useless and untimely meetings. You, however, should see whether it is not a shameful thing to give up such vices for the sake of studying Magic, yet fail to give them up for the sake of God's commandments or at least for His love.

*Curio:* I will observe them diligently, and may God turn it to a happy outcome. 

*C.:* It was altogether necessary for me to propose these things to you, since I have fallen under suspicion among the impious and wicked crowd because of them. 

*Curio:* I truly embrace them gladly; for I see already how much peace and tranquility of life they bring, even if God's commands were not a factor. 

*C.:* But observe also the rest of God’s Commandments: I have numbered at least these four, because I have a **bad reputation** <note>original: *male audio*; literally "I hear badly," a Latin idiom meaning to be spoken of poorly by others.</note> on account of them.

<summary>The teacher reveals that his "Magic" is actually just the diligent study of many arts, admitting that his complex rituals were a theatrical performance designed to keep bothersome people away and protect his privacy.</summary>

<keywords>Magic, definition of magic, Trinity, theatrical staging, reputation, commandments, curiosity, study of arts</keywords>

# INST. MAG. <note>Abbreviation for *Institutio Magisterialis* (Magisterial Instruction).</note>
<meta>Catchword: [search],</meta>

*Curio:* What, then, do I still lack? 

*C.:* Nothing, as far as I know, if you are true to yourself. For GOD, whose sun rises even upon the wicked, is never lacking to pious and honorable endeavors; the rest depends on you. 

*Curio:* And on my **<term>instructor</term>** <note>original: *institutoris*</note>. But who will that be? 

*C.:* I do not know if you truly need an instructor; perhaps a mentor and a partner in your labors. If you wish to use my help for these things, I profess that I owe such service to the **<term>Commonwealth</term>** <note>original: *Reipublicæ*</note>. 

*Curio:* Therefore, it will not be troublesome to you if I meet with you more often? 

*C.:* On the contrary, it will be a pleasure. 

*Curio:* What if I admit even more people into our society? 

*C.:* As many as you like, provided they are good and talented. 

*Curio:* We shall come to an agreement between us regarding the **<term>tuition fee</term>** <note>original: *didactro*; a term derived from Greek referring to a teacher's pay.</note>. 

*C.:* I shall do it for free, and I will even give thanks to you. 

*Curio:* If that is your mind, I no longer wonder that you rejected large stipends and have served for free until now. 

*C.:* Again you speak from the mouth of men <note>The teacher suggests Curio is thinking like the common crowd, who value things only by their monetary price.</note>. 

*Curio:* Therefore, we shall meet in this house? 

*C.:* Yes, and we shall practice declamation. 

*Curio:* And we shall weave **<term>Syllogisms</term>** <note>Logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>. 

*C.:* And we shall run through the **<term>Nomenclature</term>** <note>original: *Nomenclatorem*; a systematic list of names or terminology for all things in the natural world.</note> of things. 

*Curio:* And we shall practice the **<term>Notory Art</term>** <note>original: *Notoriam artem*; a medieval system of study intended to gain knowledge or memory through prayers and figures.</note>. 

*C.:* And we shall gaze at the **<term>stars</term>** <note>original: *sydera*</note>. 

*Curio:* And we shall measure the lands, and calculate our treasures. 

*C.:* And we shall search into nature—

<summary>The teacher and Curio agree to form a scholarly society, moving away from "magic" toward a comprehensive curriculum of logic, linguistics, astronomy, and natural science. The teacher emphasizes his commitment to the public good by refusing any tuition fees for his instruction.</summary>

<keywords>educational philosophy, tuition, Commonwealth, syllogisms, Notory Art, nomenclature, astronomy, natural philosophy, altruism</keywords>

*Christian:* Oh, that time when we have begun to know ourselves and our own capabilities!

*Curio:* Gladly, since you are so generous with your promises. 

*Christian:* May GOD grant that no useless word fall from us, that no moment of time flow away uselessly, and that no evil counselor move us away from this undertaking of ours. 

*Curio:* Farewell, Christian, and continue to laugh at the madness of men. 

*Christian:* I do so indeed, but for now

# C O N C L U S I O N . <note>original: *PERORATIO*</note>

*IF you have read through these writings of mine, **Wise reader** <note>original: *Cordate lector*</note>, which are neither plainly serious nor entirely humorous, I pray you kindly dismiss them, and do not examine them according to the standard of your more noble intellect. This is the voice of one **humble fellow** <note>original: *homuncionis*, literally "little man"; a common expression of modesty in 17th-century prefaces.</note>, long treated harshly by many, and perhaps provoked beyond the bounds of propriety. Yet there are not lacking, even among the number of the more fortunate, those who mutter such things to themselves, only to bury them again soon after under the more favorable dust of hope and expectation. Truly, just as there is a much different freedom of the tongue amidst the noise of drunks than when the sober sit together, so this noisy age of ours is more fertile and tolerant of trifles than in the past, when matters of faith and learning were treated with true gravity. **The die is cast** <note>original: *Jacta alea est*; a famous Latin phrase attributed to Julius Caesar, signifying a point of no return.</note>, with injury to no good person, I think; as for the roar of the wicked, it does not descend to posterity. There will come a time when, the **mask of the human stage** <note>original: *humanae scenae larva*; this refers to the "Theatrum Mundi" or "World Stage" concept, where life is viewed as a theatrical performance.</note> having been stripped away, we shall look upon ourselves in our naked state; then, that **hypocrisy** <note>original: *hypocrisin*</note> which for so long terrified many and exercised its tyranny will be laughed at with full and free guffaws. Meanwhile, if our present and long-lasting unhappiness has revealed in passing any of the **secrets of the world** <note>original: *arcanorum Mundi*</note>, we wish to dedicate all of it to the simpler and more credulous souls, lest they pursue the same snares, fictions, and vanities after us, and—later than the brevity of human life permits—confess that they were warned of the truth. Thus.*

<summary>This concluding address (Peroratio) serves as a modest defense of the author's work, acknowledging its mix of humor and seriousness while critiquing the hypocrisy of the age. The author expresses a hope that his revelations of the "secrets of the world" will save future readers from falling into the same intellectual traps he encountered.</summary>

<keywords>conclusion, wise reader, hypocrisy, world stage, secrets of the world, brevity of life, modesty, social critique</keywords>

# ENOUGH HAS BEEN GIVEN TO THE CHURCH, ENOUGH TO THE FATHERLAND. <note>original: *SAT ECCLESIÆ, SAT PATRIÆ DATUM*; a phrase suggesting the author has fulfilled his duty to both his faith and his country.</note>

## PASQUIN’S COMPLAINT. <note>original: *PASQ. QUERELA*. "Pasquin" refers to Pasquino, a famous "talking statue" in Rome upon which people would secretly post anonymous satirical poems or "pasquinades" criticizing the authorities.</note>

*Listen, O Nobles,* <note>original: *Proceres*, referring to leaders or those in high standing.</note> *today the pen enjoys the greatest freedom,*
*Everyone writes whatever they please.*
*Now one may praise or criticize morals without punishment,*
*So great is the favor of Pasquin to speak at length.*
*But if by chance you dare something false, or perhaps too sharp,* <note>original: *emunctius*, literally "more wiped" or "more cleaned," used metaphorically for something witty, refined, or biting.</note>
*It is snatched away, so that truth finds no place in the city.*
*Is this then the "freedom of the pen"? O empty times!*
*This is not freedom, but a heavy slavery.* <note>original: *grave servitium*</note>

->D. G.<- <note>Likely the initials of the author or a closing dedication like "Deo Gratia" (By the Grace of God).</note>

# THE END.
